sections.title: Intro
lines: Miles Home Services Marketing Playbook — Master Template

This is the trade-neutral playbook Miles runs for every home services business. It holds the system: deploy logic, offer rules, customer journey, scripts, tracking and checklists. Everything specific to one trade (seasons, offers, triggers, audiences) lives in that trade's playbook. Brackets like [TRADE], [SERVICE] and $[X] are filled per client.

sections.title: 0. How Miles uses this template
lines: Owner picks a trade. Miles loads this master plus the matching trade playbook. Multi-trade businesses load each trade playbook and split budget by margin and season.
Map the climate region from the owner's ZIPs (table below). The trade playbook's region calendar sets month-by-month priorities.
Score every ZIP (table below). Top scorers get prospecting budget; low scorers get retargeting and local search only.
Pick the offer path per ZIP: cash offer, financing offer, or skip, from the affordability check.
Build campaigns with the channel standards here and the trade playbook's service lines, negatives and offers.
Arm the journey and triggers: speed-to-lead, post-job, reviews and retention from this master; weather and event triggers from the trade playbook.
Get owner approval before anything spends or sends.

A new trade gets its own playbook built on the same 10 sections: at a glance, seasonality by region, location signals, demographics, offers, channels, triggers, after the job, compliance, deploy checklist.
New England, NY, upper Midwest, Great Lakes, northern Plains, Mountain West
Short outdoor season; freeze and heating demand dominate Nov–Mar
PA, NJ, MD, VA, Ohio Valley, KY, TN, MO, KS, NC piedmont
Two weather peaks, real freeze events, spring and fall outdoor seasons
FL, Gulf Coast, GA, SC, AL, MS, LA, East and Gulf TX
Heat and humidity dominate; hurricane season Jun–Nov; near year-round outdoor work
AZ, NV, NM, inland Southern CA, West TX
Extreme summer heat; monsoon storms Jul–Sep; winter is the outdoor season
TX, OK, KS, NE, CO, MO, IA
Mild; long rainy season; dry-season outdoor window Jun–Sep
A service area spanning two regions runs as two campaigns with two calendars.
ZIP scoring (Census ACS data per ZIP)
Older housing = more repairs and replacements
Enough volume to exit learning phase
From the trade playbook (e.g. storm history, lot size, freeze days)

Affordability check: average ticket ÷ median annual income. Low ratio → lead with the cash offer. Middle → lead with the monthly payment. High ratio and low homeownership → skip prospecting there. Thresholds are set per trade and tightened by each account's real close rates.

Trade(s) and service lines · ZIPs or radius · capacity (jobs per week, crews) · average ticket and margin per service line · financing partner and lowest payment · licenses, warranty, certifications · CRM, call tracking, booking link, review link · monthly budget and approval caps · offers the owner will not run.
Optimize to cost per booked job, not cost per lead.

Never spend, launch or message a customer list without owner approval. Once approved at setup, these run on their own: speed-to-lead text, missed-call text-back, post-job review request, no-show recovery.
Every offer carries a deadline and an expiration in the CRM.
Only claim scarcity, credentials and results that are true.

Default buyer for planned work: homeowner, age 30+, in a ZIP with median household income of $70K or more. Emergency work (burst pipe, no heat, outage) drops the income filter and starts at 25+, because anyone with a leak calls. Each trade playbook has an "Audience spec for Miles" table with the exact segments.
Planned-work ads start at 30+; most buyers are 35+
Never cap the top age; 65+ owns most and spends heavily
$70K ZIP median is the default floor
Google's "Top 50%" income tier starts near here, so a $70K floor can't be set as a Google tier
"People living in" the scored ZIP list (hard control)
Scored ZIPs or radius, presence only
Not available as a reliable US filter: the ZIP list is the income filter
Household-income tiers as bid adjustments only; never exclude "Lower 50%" or "Unknown"
"Homeowners" detailed demographic (observe, then target); exclude "Renters" on planned segments
Advantage+ hard minimum caps at 25; segment age range is a suggestion. Switch to original audience if more than 20% of spend lands under the segment minimum
ZIP scoring is the main audience tool: owner-occupied share, median income, home value and housing age decide where money goes.
Emergency segments: no income or homeowner filter, and phones must be answered before launch.
Planned segments: homeowner required, income floor from the trade spec, age from the trade spec.
Seed lookalikes and Customer Match with closed-won customers, never with all leads.
Never target or exclude by race, ethnicity, religion or other protected traits, or by proxies for them.
Home services ads use no Meta Special Ad Category. Declare Financial Products only when the ad itself is a credit or loan offer.
After 30 booked jobs, Miles compares closed-won age, ZIP and income-tier mix with the spec and proposes tighter ranges for owner approval.

Sources: Census HVS via NAHB, Q4 2025 · Census income 2024 · Harvard JCHS spending by age · homeownership by income (Urban Institute / ACS 2024) · Meta audience controls (Jon Loomer) · Google demographic targeting

sections.title: 1. Segment demand before building anything
lines: Every trade mixes these five demand types. The trade playbook says which ones it has and in what share.
Priority scheduling / diagnostic credit; never discount
Free assessment where lawful; no promised claim outcome

sections.title: 2. Offer engineering
lines: A discount is not an offer. An offer is discount + deadline + reason-why + stack + risk reversal; add financing on big tickets.
The offer ladder (every client needs all five)
Free [ESTIMATE / INSPECTION] or $[X] [DIAGNOSTIC] credited to the job
Thank-you credit on next [SERVICE]; referral reward after the friend's job
Big tickets: show dollars off. Small tickets: flat $ or percent.
Work the discount back from margin; it must cost less than acquiring a new job.
Members get standing member pricing instead of coupons.
Don't stack discounts by default. Show eligibility, exclusions, expiration and finance terms in the creative.
"Free" only when truly free. Financing claims only when the lender's terms support them.
Rotate deadlines monthly; refresh offers each season from the trade playbook.

sections.title: 3. Seasonality framework
lines: Budget follows demand; flat budgets overspend in slow months and underspend at the peak. For each client Miles builds a 12-month calendar:
Take the trade playbook's region table for the client's climate region.
Mark peak, shoulder and slow months per service line.
Launch pre-season campaigns and reactivation 3–4 weeks before each peak.
Weight budget toward peaks; keep retargeting and local search alive in slow months.
Use slow months for maintenance, memberships, reviews, SEO content and early-booking offers.
Off-season reactivation converts at roughly half the in-season rate, so time customer sends to the shoulder before each peak.

sections.title: 4. Channel standards
lines: One campaign per profit-driving service line and urgency (repair vs install); each ad lands on its matching service page.
Ad angles: price/offer, speed, trust, warranty, financing, local proof. Use city qualifiers.
Base negatives for every trade: jobs, careers, salary, school, training, DIY, how to, parts, supplies, free. Add the trade playbook's negatives. Reconcile search terms weekly.
Local Service Ads and Google Business Profile
Verify categories and service areas; answer every lead fast; dispute ineligible leads; judge on booked jobs, not billed leads.
Keep GBP categories, hours, areas, photos, services and booking link current; post job photos weekly.
One page per service and one per real service city; unique photos, FAQs, proof and a clear call/book button.
Separate install and repair pages; never land an install ad on a repair page.
Proof-led: before/after and testimonials (with consent), crew, process, financing, seasonal reminders.
Instant forms set to Higher intent; retargeting is its own campaign with its own creative.
Capture photos and 15–30 second vertical videos on every job; test one hook, visual or CTA at a time.
Small budgets consolidate; don't split $100–150/day across many ad sets.
Days 1–3 after launch: touch nothing. First honest read days 4–7.
Pause losers and shift budget only inside owner-set caps, with approval and one-click revert.
Exclude current customers and recent submitters from prospecting.

sections.title: 5. Landing page wireframe
lines: Trust strip: license/insurance, current rating, warranty (only if true)
Hero: real job photo + offer + call and book buttons
Problem → solution → process → local before/after gallery
Scope: included and excluded work, financing, timeline, FAQs
Form: name, phone, ZIP, job type, preferred date, consent text
Sticky mobile call/book button; source-aware thank-you page; call tracking number

sections.title: 6. Lead capture and speed-to-lead
lines: The most expensive thing in a home services account is the time before someone calls the lead back.
Text in under 60 seconds with booking link; call task to CSR
"Sorry we missed you, how can we help?" + booking link
Assign rep; no call in 5 min → reassign + notify manager
Day 1 text, Day 3 email with financing, Day 7 deadline reminder
Offer the open slot to recent estimate holders
New lead 1 day, contacted 3, estimate 7 → task, then escalate
Code reason: no answer, price, timing, area, capacity, competitor
Phone and form leads are different products; give them different cost targets.

sections.title: 7. After the job: thank-you coupon, review request, referral
lines: Trigger: job complete or invoice paid. Stop the review sequence as soon as a review is detected.

Compliance rule: the coupon is a thank-you for the job, never payment for a review. Every customer gets the coupon whether or not they review, and every customer gets the review link whatever score they gave. The FTC Consumer Review Rule bans incentives tied to review sentiment and bans review suppression; Google's policy bans incentivized reviews.
Quality check, photos (with consent), care tips, tech handoff line
Thank-you + coupon: $[X] off your next [SERVICE], code [CODE], valid through [DATE]
All customers; code tracked in CRM
Honest review request with direct link
Everyone; scores 1–6 also open a manager service-recovery task
Referral: friend saves $[X], you get $[Y] after their job is completed
Check-in + maintenance plan / next service offer

Review responses: 4–5 stars get a reply within 24 hours (rotate templates, name the service and town). 1–3 stars never get an auto-reply; the owner approves a drafted response that acknowledges, takes it offline and fixes it.
Coupon rules: one unique code per customer; 6–12 month expiry; minimum spend and exclusions stated; not stackable; members get member pricing instead.

sections.title: 8. Retention plays
lines: Day 1: "We're booking [SEASON] [SERVICE] and you came to mind" → Day 3: "Should I take you off the list?" → Day 7: offer with deadline
"Most customers book their annual [SERVICE] around now. Want your old time slot?"
6 touches over 21 days: hook → SMS → offer → scarcity (if true) → local story → break-up
Exit anyone who books or has an open estimate
Email with "you saved $X" → SMS link → call task → win-back
+30 days feedback ask → +60 offer → +90 long-term drip
SMS offer → email detail → SMS deadline
"Recent work near [NEIGHBORHOOD]" photos, yard signs, postcards where permitted

sections.title: 9. Script bank
lines: Missed-call text: Hi [FIRST NAME], this is [REP] with [BUSINESS]. Sorry we missed you. Are you looking for help with [SERVICE]? Reply here or call [PHONE]. Reply STOP to opt out.
Speed-to-lead text: Hi [FIRST NAME], thanks for reaching out to [BUSINESS] about [SERVICE]. Grab a time here: [BOOKING LINK], or reply with the best time to call.

Estimate follow-up: Hi [FIRST NAME], thanks for considering [BUSINESS] for [PROJECT]. Your estimate: [LINK]. Happy to answer questions on scope, timing or [FINANCING]. Would [OPTION A] or [OPTION B] work to talk next steps?
Tech handoff (at the door): We appreciate you choosing [BUSINESS]. You may get a message asking for honest feedback on today's work. We value all feedback and want to hear any concerns directly too.

Thank-you coupon SMS: Hi [FIRST NAME], thank you for trusting [BUSINESS] with your [SERVICE]. Here's [$X OFF] your next [SERVICE]: code [CODE], valid through [DATE]. Terms: [LINK]. No review or referral required.
Review SMS: Thanks for choosing [BUSINESS], [FIRST NAME]. If you have a moment, would you share your honest experience? [REVIEW LINK]. It helps other local homeowners.

Review email: Subject: How was your experience with [BUSINESS]? Body: Hi [FIRST NAME], thanks for trusting us with [SERVICE]. We welcome your honest feedback, positive or negative, at [LINK]. For a service concern, contact [SUPPORT] and we'll make it right.
Private service check: Hi [FIRST NAME], just checking [SERVICE] is working as expected. If anything needs attention, reply here or call [NUMBER].
Referral: Know someone who needs [SERVICE]? Share [FRIEND CODE] and they save [Y] in [CREDIT]. No online review required.
Reactivation: Hey [FIRST NAME], it's [NAME] from [BUSINESS]. We're booking [SEASON] [SERVICE] and you came to mind. Want a quote?

sections.title: 10. CRM pipeline and fields
lines: Stages: New lead → Contact attempted → Qualified → Appointment booked → Estimate sent → Won/scheduled → Work complete/invoiced → Repeat/referral → Lost/unqualified. Timestamp every stage.
utm_source, utm_campaign, gclid, tracking number, first touch, last touch
Quoted, sold and invoiced revenue, direct costs, contribution margin
Offer code, offer type, expiry, redeemed
Open complaint, job complete, review invite sent, opt-out, do-not-contact
What was installed or serviced, date, warranty end, next recommended service
CSR owner, speed to lead, call disposition, booked status, reason lost
Use the contractor's field-service software as the source of truth when it exists; call tracking for inbound calls; the CRM for automations. All SMS/email needs consent and opt-out handling.

sections.title: 11. Economics, KPIs and reporting
lines: Work backwards from the job, never forwards from a budget.
Share of gross profit the owner will spend to win a job
Allowable cost per sold job × lead-to-sold rate
Gross-profit target ÷ gross profit per job
Jobs needed × allowable cost per sold job; check against market size
Revenue − direct job costs − acquisition spend
Median minutes from lead to first contact
Sanity check before quoting numbers: $5,000 spend at $2,000 CAC = 2.5 customers, not 10. Confirm what CPA means first.
Missed calls, unanswered leads, urgent jobs, pending estimates
Spend, qualified leads, bookings, sold jobs, cost per booked job, objections
Revenue, gross profit, CAC, source quality, repeats, redemptions

sections.title: 12. Client operations
lines: Check the phones before blaming the ads. Audit speed to lead and booked rate before touching budget.
Listen before changing. First 30 days: learn the owner's business; lead recommendations with the owner's own words.
Test small, then scale. Move 10% of budget for 30 days to prove a change.
Set the cost-per-job range up front. Honest ranges before launch keep clients longer.
Copy winners across accounts in the same trade and market type.
One-page expectation agreement: what marketing controls, what CSR/sales/ops own, lead definitions, how results mature.
Weekly 15-minute check-in per client: data issues, test result, next action, deadline; keep a change log.
Sales QA: sample real calls; score speed, booking attempts, objection handling.

sections.title: 13. 90-day rollout
lines: Audit spend, calls, CRM, market, margins, site, offers, review process
Baseline + tracking map + approved offer terms
Fix conversion paths, build 1–2 offers, launch missed-call and estimate follow-up
Live campaigns + QA of 10 sample leads
Post-job thank-you, reviews, loyalty/referral, local SEO
Expand proven segments, improve close rate, rebudget by gross profit

sections.title: 14. Client brief (fill one per client)
lines: Service lines (top 3 by margin, with ticket and margin)
Service area (ZIPs / radius) and climate region
Capacity (jobs per week, crews, seasonal limits)
Licenses, warranty, certifications, years in business
Financing partner and lowest monthly payment
CRM / field-service software, call tracking, booking link, review link
Current baseline (spend, CPL, booking %, close %, CAC, reviews)
Monthly budget and caps (max daily move %, floor, ceiling)
Offer limits (max discount, min ticket, exclusions)
Business target (monthly jobs, revenue, gross profit)
Speed-to-lead, missed-call, review request, no-show texts

sections.title: 15. Campaign brief and launch checklist
lines: GOAL: [X] paying customers at CAC ≤ $[X]; revenue [X]; margin [X]
CHANNEL: [SEARCH / LSA / SEO / META] | BUDGET: $[X] | LANDING URL: [URL]
CTA: [CALL / GET ESTIMATE / BOOK] | TRACKING: [NUMBER / UTMS / CRM]
TEST: Control [A]; Challenger [B]; metric [COST PER SOLD JOB]
STOP/GO: review after [N] qualified leads or [N] closed jobs
☐ Trade playbook loaded; climate region and ZIP scores set
☐ Claims, discounts, finance terms and expiration approved
☐ Call routing, live pickup and after-hours plan tested
☐ Forms, UTMs, conversion events and CRM job IDs tested
☐ GBP / LSA categories and campaign relevance checked
☐ Thank-you, review and loyalty workflows kept separate; no review rewards or gating
☐ Coupon codes unique, tracked, capped, non-stackable
☐ Consent, opt-outs and referral terms reviewed
☐ Trade triggers armed; reporting owners assigned

Never spend, launch or message a customer list without owner approval.
Once approved at setup, these run on their own: speed-to-lead text, missed-call text-back, post-job review request, no-show recovery.
Every offer carries a deadline and an expiration in the CRM.
Only claim scarcity, credentials and results that are true.
